questions.question: A team with a strong delivery record cannot segment a metric decline, cannot defend its inherited metric definition, and has an 18% identity gap in its event data. The leader hires two experienced shipping PMs. What is the most likely result?
options: Balanced improvement, since more senior capacity helps every area
The measurement gap closes gradually as the new PMs encounter it
More of the same work, faster — and if the missing capability is the one that chooses what to build, the error gets larger
Delivery slows temporarily during onboarding, then improves overall
questions.explanation: Capacity added to an existing capability set produces more of the same output. B is the tempting answer because good PMs do notice gaps, but noticing is depth 1; nobody in this team can do the measurement work, so encountering it changes nothing except who is frustrated by it.

questions.question: Which of these is stated as a capability rather than a trait?
options: Can define a metric's population, event, window, and aggregation, and defend it against challenge
Is data-driven and comfortable with ambiguity
Has five years of experience in a similar product category
Is a strong communicator who builds trust across functions
questions.explanation: A names something observable in an artifact or a decision, so two people can check it. D is the tempting one — communication really is load-bearing for a PM, but as written it can only be felt, which is how hiring in your own image survives review. Restate it as "can write a decision memo an executive acts on without a meeting".

questions.question: A leader plans to close a measurement gap by developing an existing PM into it. What single check most determines whether this will work?
options: Whether the PM is motivated and has asked for the growth
Whether there is a real decision, with a real consequence, that the PM will hold while developing
Whether a course or a mentor is available
Whether the PM is at depth 1 rather than depth 0
questions.explanation: Development without a decision to practise on produces recognition and then stalls. A and C are tempting because motivation and support genuinely help, and their absence would sink the plan too — but with both present and no real decision attached, you get reading and shadowing, which is depth 1 dressed up as depth 3.

questions.question: A team says it can get analysis from a central data team when it needs it. What makes this a real interface rather than a hope?
options: A shared channel and a good working relationship
A history of the data team helping when asked
An agreement that the data team will prioritize product requests
A named person, an agreed latency, and an agreed evidence standard
questions.explanation: Without those three, the queue silently sets your evidence standard: when the wait is four weeks and the decision is due in two, the team decides on what it has and records nothing about the standard it missed. A and B describe goodwill, which is real and which evaporates precisely when the other team is busy.

questions.question: A leader hires against a genuine gap — someone whose strengths nobody else on the team has. Six months later that person is isolated and considered a poor fit. What was most likely missed?
options: The gap was not real, and the team's original instincts were correct
The translation surface — a decision they own, a forum their work lands in, an artifact the team already reads
Cultural screening during the interview process
The hire was too senior for the team's stage
questions.explanation: Complementary hiring has a bill: someone unlike the team has no natural advocate and no way to demonstrate value inside existing rituals. A is the conclusion the team itself will reach, which is why it is the dangerous one — it retires the gap without ever testing it, and the next hire will be someone more like everyone else.
